entries.a4d28f6b228bed8588bdd4d32bf6bc7b5806f477: <div sID="gen12543" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="113" osisID="Ps.113" sID="Ps.113"/> <div eID="gen12543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12544" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12545" type="x-p"/> This psalm begins and ends with "Hallelujah;" for, as many others, it is designed to promote the great and good work of praising God. I. We are here called upon and urged to praise God, <reference osisRef="Ps.113.1-Ps.113.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. We are here furnished with matter for praise, and words are put into our mouths, in singing which we must with holy fear and love give to God the glory of, 1. The elevations of his glory and greatness, <reference osisRef="Ps.113.4-Ps.113.5">ver. 4, 5</reference>. 2. The condescensions of his grace and goodness (<reference osisRef="Ps.113.6-Ps.113.9">ver. 6-9</reference>), which very much illustrate one another, that we may be duly affected with both.
entries.d9a7f14485c1fbda00c51a8db45eec1c48044089: <div eID="gen12545" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12544" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">A Call to Praise God; God's Greatness and Condescension.</title> <div sID="gen12546" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Praise ye the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . Praise, O ye servants of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , praise the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">2</hi> Blessed be the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> from this time forth and for evermore. <hi type="super">3</hi> From the rising of the sun unto the going down of the same the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's name <hi type="italic">is</hi> to be praised. <hi type="super">4</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> high above all nations, <hi type="italic">and</hi> his glory above the heavens. <hi type="super">5</hi> Who <hi type="italic">is</hi> like unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God, who dwelleth on high, <hi type="super">6</hi> Who humbleth <hi type="italic">himself</hi> to behold <hi type="italic">the things that are</hi> in heaven, and in the earth! <hi type="super">7</hi> He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, <hi type="italic">and</hi> lifteth the needy out of the dunghill; <hi type="super">8</hi> That he may set <hi type="italic">him</hi> with princes, <hi type="italic">even</hi> with the princes of his people. <hi type="super">9</hi> He maketh the barren woman to keep house, <hi type="italic">and to be</hi> a joyful mother of children. Praise ye the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen12546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12547" type="x-p"/> In this psalm, <div eID="gen12547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12548" type="x-p"/> I. We are extorted to give glory to God, to give him the glory due to his name. <div eID="gen12548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12549" type="x-p"/> 1. The invitation is very pressing: <hi type="italic">praise you the Lord,</hi> and again and again, <hi type="italic">Praise him, praise him; blessed be his name,</hi> for it is to be praised, <reference osisRef="Ps.113.1-Ps.113.3">v. 1-3</reference>. This intimates, (1.) That it is a necessary and most excellent duty, greatly pleasing to God, and has a large room in religion. (2.) That it is a duty we should much abound in, in which we should be frequently employed and greatly enlarged. (3.) That it is work which we are very backward to, and which we need to be engaged and excited to by precept upon precept and line upon line. (4.) That those who are much in praising God themselves will court others to it, both because they find the weight of the work, and that there is need of all the help they can fetch in (there is employment for all hearts, all hands, and all little enough), and because they find the pleasure of it, which they wish all their friends may share in. <div eID="gen12549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12550" type="x-p"/> 2. The invitation is very extensive. Observe, (1.) From whom God has praise—from his own people; they are here called upon to praise God, as those that will answer the call: <hi type="italic">Praise, O you servants of the Lord!</hi> They have most reason to praise him; for those that attend him as his servants know him best and receive most of his favours. And it is their business to praise him; that is the work required of them as his servants: it is easy pleasant work to speak well of their Master, and do him what honour they can; if they do not, who should? Some understand it of the Levites; but, if so, all Christians are a royal priesthood, <hi type="italic">to show forth the praises of him that has called them,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.9">1 Pet. ii. 9</reference>. The angels are the servants of the Lord; they need not be called upon by us to praise God, yet it is a comfort to us that they do praise him, and that they praise him better than we can. (2.) From whom he ought to have praise. [1.] From all ages (<reference osisRef="Ps.113.2">v. 2</reference>)—<hi type="italic">from this time forth for evermore.</hi> Let not this work die with us, but let us be doing it in a better world, and let those that come after us be doing it in this. Let not our seed degenerate, but let God be praised through all the generations of time, and not in this only. We must bless the Lord in our day, by saying, with the psalmist, <hi type="italic">Blessed be his name now and always.</hi> [2.] From all places—<hi type="italic">from the rising of the sun to the going down of the same,</hi> that is, throughout the habitable world. Let all that enjoy the benefit of the sun rising (and those that do so must count upon it that the sun will set) give thanks for that light to the Father of lights. God's <hi type="italic">name is to be praised;</hi> it ought to be praised by all nations; for in every place, from east to west, there appear the manifest proofs and products of his wisdom, power, and goodness; and it is to be lamented that so great a part of mankind are ignorant of him, and give that praise to others which is due to him alone. But perhaps there is more in it; as the <reference osisRef="Ps.113.2">former verse</reference> gave us a glimpse of the kingdom of glory, intimating that God's name shall be <hi type="italic">blessed for ever</hi> (when time shall be no more that praise shall be the work of heaven), so this verse gives us a glimpse of the kingdom of grace in the gospel-dispensation of it. When the church shall no longer be confined to the Jewish nation, but shall spread itself all the world over, when in <hi type="italic">every place</hi> spiritual <hi type="italic">incense shall be offered to our God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mal.1.11">Mal. i. 11</reference>), then from <hi type="italic">the rising to the setting of the sun the Lord's name shall be praised</hi> by some in all countries. <div eID="gen12550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12551" type="x-p"/> II. We are here directed what to give him the glory of. <div eID="gen12551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12552" type="x-p"/> 1. Let us look up with an eye of faith, and see how high his glory is in the upper world, and mention that to his praise, <reference osisRef="Ps.113.4-Ps.113.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. We are, in our praises, to exalt his name, for he is high, his glory is high. (1.) <hi type="italic">High above all nations,</hi> their kings though ever so pompous, their people though ever so numerous. Whether it be true of an earthly king or no that though he is <hi type="italic">major singulis—greater than individuals,</hi> he is <hi type="italic">minor universis—less than the whole,</hi> we will not dispute; but we are sure it is not true of the King of kings. Put all the nations together, and he is above them all; they are before him as the <hi type="italic">drop of the bucket and the small dust of the balance,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.60.15">Isa. lx. 15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.60.17">17</reference>. Let all nations think and speak highly of God, for he is high above them all. (2.) High <hi type="italic">above the heavens;</hi> the throne of his glory is in the highest heavens, which should raise our hearts in praising him, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.41">Lam. iii. 41</reference>. <hi type="italic">His glory is above the heavens,</hi> that is, above the angels; he is above what they are, for their brightness is nothing to his,—above what they do, for they are under his command and do his pleasure,—and above what even they can speak him to be. He is exalted above <hi type="italic">all blessing and praise,</hi> not only all ours, but all theirs. We must therefore say, with holy admiration, <hi type="italic">Who is like unto the Lord our God?</hi> who of all the princes and potentates of the earth? who of all the bright and blessed spirits above? None can equal him, none dare compare with him. God is to be praised as transcendently, incomparably, and infinitely great; for he <hi type="italic">dwells on high,</hi> and from on high sees all, and rules all, and justly attracts all praise to himself. <div eID="gen12552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12553" type="x-p"/> 2. Let us look around with an eye of observation, and see how extensive his goodness is in the lower world, and mention that to his praise. He is a God <hi type="italic">who exalts himself to dwell, who humbles himself in heaven, and in earth.</hi> Some think there is a transposition, <hi type="italic">He exalts himself to dwell in heaven,</hi> he <hi type="italic">humbles himself to behold on earth;</hi> but the sense is plain enough as we take it, only observe, God is said to <hi type="italic">exalt himself</hi> and to <hi type="italic">humble himself,</hi> both are his own act and deed; as he is self-existent, so he is both the fountain of his own honour and the spring of his own grace; God's condescending goodness appears, <div eID="gen12553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12554" type="x-p"/> (1.) In the cognizance he takes of the world below him. His glory is <hi type="italic">above the nations</hi> and <hi type="italic">above the heavens,</hi> and yet neither is neglected by him. <hi type="italic">God is great,</hi> yet <hi type="italic">he despises not any,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.36.5">Job xxxvi. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">He humbles himself to behold</hi> all his creatures, all his subjects, though he is infinitely above them. Considering the infinite perfection, sufficiency, and felicity of the divine nature, it must be acknowledged as an act of wonderful condescension that God is pleased to take into the thoughts of his eternal counsel, and into the hand of his universal Providence, both the armies of heaven and the inhabitants of the earth (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.35">Dan. iv. 35</reference>); even in this dominion he humbles himself. [1.] It is condescension in him to behold the things in heaven, to support the beings, direct the motions, and accept the praises and services, of the angels themselves; for he needs them not, nor is benefited by them. [2.] Much more is it condescension in him to <hi type="italic">behold the things that are in the earth,</hi> to visit the sons of men, and regard them, to order and overrule their affairs, and to take notice of what they say and do, that he may fill the earth with his goodness, and so set us an example of stooping to do good, of taking notice of, and concerning ourselves about, our inferiors. If it be such condescension for God to behold things in heaven and earth, what an amazing condescension was it for the Son of God to come from heaven to earth and take our nature upon him, that he might <hi type="italic">seek and save those that were lost!</hi> Herein indeed he humbled himself. <div eID="gen12554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12555" type="x-p"/> (2.) In the particular favour he sometimes shows to the least and lowest of the inhabitants of this meaner lower world. He not only beholds the great things in the earth, but the meanest, and those things which great men commonly overlook. Not does he merely behold them, but does wonders for them, and things that are very surprising, out of the common road of providence and chain of causes, which shows that the world is governed, not by a course of nature, for that would always run in the same channel, but by a God of nature, who delights in doing things we looked not for. [1.] Those that have been long despicable are sometimes, on a sudden, made honourable (<reference osisRef="Ps.113.78">v. 7, 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">He raises up the poor out of the dust, that he may set him with princes. First,</hi> Thus God does sometimes magnify himself, and his own wisdom, power, and sovereignty. When he has some great work to do he chooses to employ those in it that were least likely, and least thought of for it by themselves or others, to the highest post of honour: Gideon is fetched from threshing, Saul from seeking the asses, and David from keeping the sheep; the apostles are sent from fishing to be <hi type="italic">fishers of men.</hi> The treasure of the gospel is put into earthen vessels, and the weak and foolish ones of the world are pitched upon to be preachers of it, to confound the <hi type="italic">wise and mighty</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.27-1Cor.1.28">1 Cor. i. 27, 28</reference>), that the excellency of the power may be of God, and all may see that promotion comes from him. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Thus God does sometimes reward the eminent piety and patience of his people who have long groaned under the burden of poverty and disgrace. When Joseph's virtue was tried and manifested he was raised from the prison-dust and <hi type="italic">set with princes.</hi> Those that are wise will observe such returns of Providence, and will understand by them <hi type="italic">the loving-kindness of the Lord.</hi> Some have applied this to the work of redemption by Jesus Christ, and not unfitly; for through him poor fallen men are raised out of the dust (one of the Jewish rabbies applies it to the resurrection of the dead), nay, out of the dunghill of sin, and <hi type="italic">set among princes,</hi> among angels, those princes of his people. Hannah had sung to this purport, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.6-1Sam.2.8">1 Sam. ii. 6-8</reference>. [2.] Those that have been long barren are sometimes, on a sudden, made fruitful, <reference osisRef="Ps.113.9">v. 9</reference>. This may look back to Sarah and Rebecca, Rachel, Hannah, and Samson's mother, or forward to Elizabeth; and many such instances there have been, in which God has looked on the affliction of his handmaids and taken away their reproach. <hi type="italic">He makes the barren woman to keep house,</hi> not only builds up the family, but thereby finds the heads of the family something to do. Note, Those that have the comfort of a family must take the care of it; <hi type="italic">bearing children</hi> and <hi type="italic">guiding the house</hi> are put together, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.14">1 Tim. v. 14</reference>. When God <hi type="italic">sets the barren in a family</hi> he expects that she should <hi type="italic">look well to the ways of her household,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.31.27">Prov. xxxi. 27</reference>. She is said to <hi type="italic">be a joyful mother of children,</hi> not only because, even in common cases, the pain is forgotten, <hi type="italic">for joy that a man-child is born into the world,</hi> but there is particular joy when a child is born to those that have been long childless (as <reference osisRef="Luke.1.14">Luke i. 14</reference>) and therefore there ought to be particular thanksgiving. <hi type="italic">Praise you the Lord.</hi> Yet, in this case, <hi type="italic">rejoice with trembling;</hi> for, though the sorrowful mother be made joyful, the joyful mother may be made sorrowful again, if the children be either removed from her or embittered to her. This, therefore, may be applied to the gospel-church among the Gentiles (the building of which is illustrated by this similitude, <reference osisRef="Isa.54.1">Isa. liv. 1</reference>, <hi type="italic">Sing, O barren! thou that didst not bear,</hi> and <reference osisRef="Gal.4.27">Gal. iv. 27</reference>), for which we, who, being sinners of the Gentiles, are children of the desolate, have reason to say, <hi type="italic">Praise you the Lord.</hi>  <chapter eID="Ps.113"/> <div eID="gen12555" type="x-p"/>

entries.881174c404802072880bdf7c29058a6f9898e6c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6825"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 113</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.113.1-Ps.113.9">Psa 113:1-9</reference>. God's majesty contrasted with His condescension and gracious dealings towards the humble furnish matter and a call for praise. The Jews, it is said, used this and Psalms 114-118 on their great festivals, and called them the Greater Hallel, or Hymn.</title> <div sID="gen10482" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6825"/>1-3. Earnestness and zeal are denoted by the emphatic repetitions.<div eID="gen10482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10483" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">servants of the Lord--</hi>or, all the people of God.<div eID="gen10483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10484" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">name of the Lord--</hi>perfections (<reference osisRef="Ps.5.11">Psa 5:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.111.9">111:9</reference>). <div eID="gen10484" type="x-p"/>
entries.6ea050935395df66db3da2ded26d8d0dfd608872: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6827"/><div sID="gen10486" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6827"/>4-6. God's exaltation enhances His condescension; <div eID="gen10486" type="x-p"/>
entries.ecfea42152c3469ac2f254473fd8d1332f0c1365: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6828"/><div sID="gen10487" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6828"/>7-8. which condescension is illustrated as often in raising the worthy poor and needy to honor (compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.8">1Sa 2:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.44.25">Psa 44:25</reference>). <div eID="gen10487" type="x-p"/>
entries.1960cb9d16436463a9bf810d87ed7dd569e98eaa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6829"/><div sID="gen10488" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6829"/>9. On this special case, compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.21">1Sa 2:21</reference>. Barrenness was regarded as a disgrace, and is a type of a deserted Church (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.1">Is 54:1</reference>).<div eID="gen10488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10489" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the barren woman ... house--</hi>literally, "the barren of the house," so that the supplied words may be omitted. <chapter eID="Ps.113"/>

entries.568a53d44750330062836ddc984af66f132f368a: <div eID="gen22522" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen22523" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22524" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22524" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22523" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22525" type="x-p"/> An exhortation to bless God for his own excellencies, <reference osisRef="Psa.113.1-Psa.113.6">Psa 113:1-6</reference>; and for his great mercy to the poor and necessitous, <reference osisRef="Psa.113.7-Psa.113.9">Psa 113:7-9</reference>. <reference osisRef="Psa.113.1-Psa.113.9">Psa 113:1-9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.114.1-Psa.114.8">Psa 114:1-8</reference>, 115, 116, <reference osisRef="Psa.117.1-Psa.117.2">Psa 117:1-2</reference>, and 118, form the great Hallel, and were sung by the Jews on their most solemn festivals, and particularly at the passover. To these reference is made by the evangelists, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.30">Mat 26:30</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Mar.14.26">Mar 14:26</reference>, there called the hymn which Jesus and his disciples sung at the passover, for the whole of the Psalms were considered as one grand hymn or thanksgiving. It was probably composed after the return from the captivity. It has no title but Hallelujah in the Hebrew and ancient Versions. <div eID="gen22525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22526" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen22526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22527" type="x-p"/> Praise, O ye servants - Probably an address to the Levites. The Anglo-Saxon has praise the Lord, ye knaves. Knapa or knave signified among our ancestors a servant; sometimes a male, a young man.
entries.c39796557100214639015e9acb2e09600b176f22: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen22527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22528" type="x-p"/> From the rising of the sun - From morning to evening be always employed in the work. Or it may be a call on all mankind to praise God for his innumerable mercies to the human race. Praise him from one end of the world unto the other. And therefore the psalmist adds,
entries.570ca4196ff97bf43af1aa65c89c79f0fe67dac9: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen22528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22529" type="x-p"/> The Lord is high above all nations - He governs all, he provides for all; therefore let all give him praise.
entries.6e8f5d3c6e7cb9b04d6e186ff105c43cd1c1aaee: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen22529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22530" type="x-p"/> Who is like unto the Lord - Those who are highly exalted are generally unapproachable; they are proud and overbearing; or so surrounded with magnificence and flatterers, that to them the poor have no access; but God, though infinitely exalted, humbleth himself to behold even heaven itself, and much more does he humble himself when he condescends to behold earth and her inhabitants; (<reference osisRef="Psa.113.6">Psa 113:6</reference>). But so does he love his creatures that he rejoices over even the meanest of them to do them good.
entries.e32e6fdc0bed63b9b11b0f23a047f9c67ed5dc1c: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen22530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22531" type="x-p"/> He raiseth up the poor - The poorest man, in the meanest and most abject circumstances, is an object of his merciful regards. He may here allude to the wretched state of the captives in Babylon, whom God raised up out of that dust and dunghill. Others apply it to the resurreetion of the dead.
entries.cd7d1205b43db846e8d28a4d3cb88f330464ae3d: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen22531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22532" type="x-p"/> With the princes - נדיבים nedebim, very properly translated by the Anglo-Saxon, the aldermen, the most respectable of his people.
entries.d0ad2f2885416e06bd19cb76709918488a28f464: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen22532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22533" type="x-p"/> He maketh the barren woman to keep house - This is a figure to point out the desolate, decreasing state of the captives in Babylon, and the happy change which took place on their return to their own land. These are nearly the words of Hannah, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.5">1Sam 2:5</reference>.  <chapter eID="Ps.113"/> <div eID="gen22533" type="x-p"/>

entries.bf21afe75bb8b833c84bb9d63f57a170f5dd2a8b: <div eID="gen10082" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Hallelujah to Him Who Raiseth Out of Low Estate</title> <div sID="gen10083" type="x-p"/> With this Psalm begins the <hi type="italic">Hallel</hi>, which is recited at the three great feasts, at the feast of the Dedication (<hi type="italic">Chanucca</hi>) and at the new moons, and not on New Year’s day and the day of Atonement, because a cheerful song of praise does not harmonize with the mournful solemnity of these days. And they are recited only in fragments during the last days of the Passover, for “my creatures, saith the Holy One, blessed be He, were drowned in the sea, and ought ye to break out into songs of rejoicing?” In the family celebration of the Passover night it is divided into two parts, the one half, <reference osisRef="Ps.113.1-Ps.113.9">Psa 113:1-9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.114.1-Ps.114.8">Psa 114:1-8</reference>, being sung before the repast, before the emptying of the second festal cup, and the other half, <reference osisRef="Ps.115.1">Psa 115:1</reference>, after the repast, after the filling of the fourth cup, to which the humnee'santes (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.30">Mat 26:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.14.26">Mar 14:26</reference>) after the institution of the Lord’s Supper, which was connected with the fourth festal cup, may refer. Paulus Burgensis styles <reference osisRef="Ps.113.1">Psa 113:1</reference> <hi type="italic">Alleluja Judaeorum magnum</hi>. This designation is also frequently found elsewhere. But according to the prevailing custom, <reference osisRef="Ps.113.1">Psa 113:1</reference>, and more particularly <reference osisRef="Ps.115.1">Psa 115:1</reference>, are called only <hi type="italic">Hallel</hi>, and Ps 136, with its “for His mercy endureth for ever” repeated twenty-six times, bears the name of “<hi type="italic">the Great Hallel</hi>” (הלּל הגּדול).<note placement="foot">Vid., the tractate <hi type="italic">Sofrim</hi>, xviii. §2. Apart from the new moons, at which the recitation of the <hi type="italic">Hallel</hi> κατ ̓ ἐξοχήν, i.e., Psalms 113-118, is only according to custom (מנהג), not according to the law, the <hi type="italic">Hallel</hi> was recited eighteen times a year during the continuance of the Temple (and in Palestine even in the present day), viz., once at the Passover, once at Shabuoth, eight times at Succoth, eight times at Chanucca (the feast of the Dedication); and now in the Exile twenty-one times, because the Passover and Succoth have received two feast-days and Shabuoth one as an addition, viz., twice at the Passover, twice at Shabuoth, nine times at Succoth. Instead of <hi type="italic">Hallel</hi> absolutely we also find the appellation “the Egyptian Hallel” (הלּל המּצרי) for Psalms 113-118. The ancient ritual only makes a distinction between this (Egyptian) Hallel and the Great Hallel, Ps 136 (see there).</note> <div eID="gen10083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10084" type="x-p"/> A heaping up, without example elsewhere, of the so-called <hi type="italic">Chirek compaginis</hi> is peculiar to <reference osisRef="Ps.113.1">Psa 113:1</reference>-9. Gesenius and others call the connecting vowels <hi type="italic">i</hi> and <hi type="italic">o</hi> (in proper names also <hi type="italic">u</hi>) the remains of old case terminations; with the former the Arabic genitive termination is compared, and with the latter the Arabic nominative termination. But in opposition to this it has been rightly observed, that this <hi type="italic">i</hi> and <hi type="italic">o</hi> are not attached to the dependent word (the genitive), but to the governing word. According to the more probable view of Ewald, §211, <hi type="italic">i</hi> and <hi type="italic">o</hi> are equivalent connecting vowels which mark the relation of the genitive case, and are to be explained from the original oneness of the Semitic and Indo-Germanic languages. <div eID="gen10084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10085" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">i</hi> is found most frequently appended to the first member of the <hi type="italic">stat. constr</hi>., and both to the <hi type="italic">masc</hi>., viz., in <reference osisRef="Deut.33.16">Deu 33:16</reference>; Zec 11:17 (perhaps twice, vid., Köhler <hi type="italic">in loc</hi>.), and to the <hi type="italic">femin</hi>., viz., in <reference osisRef="Gen.31.39">Gen 31:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.110.4">Psa 110:4</reference>; Isa 1:21. <reference osisRef="Lev.26.42">Lev 26:42</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.116.1">Psa 116:1</reference> hardly belong here. Then this <hi type="italic">i</hi>is also frequently found when the second member of the <hi type="italic">stat. constr.</hi> has a preposition, and this preposition is consequently in process of being resolved: <reference osisRef="Gen.49.11">Gen 49:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.15.6">Exo 15:6</reference>, Oba 1:3 (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.16">Jer 49:16</reference>), Hos 10:11; <reference osisRef="Lam.1.1">Lam 1:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.123.1">Psa 123:1</reference>, and perhaps Sol 1:9. Also in the <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi>, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.23">Jer 22:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.13">Jer 51:13</reference>; Eze 27:3. Thirdly, where a word stands between the two notions that belong together according to the genitival relation, and the <hi type="italic">stat. construct. </hi>is consequently really resolved: <reference osisRef="Ps.101.5">Psa 101:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.16">Isa 22:16</reference>; Mic 7:14. It is the same <hi type="italic">i</hi> which is found in a great many proper names, both Israelitish, e.g., <hi type="italic">Gamaliel</hi> (benefit of God), and Phoenician, e.g., <hi type="italic">Melchizedek, Hanniba‛al</hi> (the favour of Baal), and is also added to many Hebrew prepositions, like בּלתּי (where the <hi type="italic">i</hi> however can, according to the context, also be a pronominal suffix), זוּלתי (where <hi type="italic">i</hi> can likewise be a suffix), מנּי (poetical). In אפסי, on the other hand, the <hi type="italic">i</hi> is always a suffix. The tone of the <hi type="italic">i</hi> only retreats in accordance with rhythmical rule (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.110.4">Psa 110:4</reference>), otherwise <hi type="italic">i</hi> is always accented. <reference osisRef="Ps.112.8">Psa 112:8</reference> shows how our <reference osisRef="Ps.113.1-Ps.113.9">Psa 113:1-9</reference> in particular delights in this ancient <hi type="italic">i</hi>, where it is even affixed to the infinitive as an ornament, a thing which occurs nowhere else, so that להושׁיבי excites the suspicion of being written in error for להושׁיבו. <div eID="gen10085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10086" type="x-p"/> Among those things which make God worthy to be praised the Psalm gives prominence to the condescension of the infinitely exalted One towards the lowly one. It is the lowliness of God lowering itself fro the exaltation of the lowly which performs its utmost in the work of redemption. Thus it becomes explicable that Mary in her <hi type="italic">Magnificat</hi> breaks forth into the same strain with the song of Hannah (1 Sam. 2) and this Psalm.
entries.f19da1448c40784e7446b1a1c08189bc69e03517: <reference osisRef="Ps.113.1-Ps.113.3">Psa 113:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen10086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10087" type="x-p"/> The call, not limited by any addition as in <reference osisRef="Ps.134.1">Psa 134:1</reference>, or eve, after the manner of Psa 103:20., extended over the earth, is given to the whole of the true Israel that corresponds to its election by grace and is faithful to its mission; and its designation by “servants of Jahve” (Ps 69:37, cf. Ps 34:23), or even “servant of Jahve” (<reference osisRef="Ps.136.22">Psa 136:22</reference>), has come into vogue more especially through the second part of Isaiah. This Israel is called upon to praise Jahve; for the praise and celebration of His Name, i.e., of His nature, which is disclosed by means of its manifestation, is a principal element, yea, the proper ground and aim, of the service, and shall finally become that which fills all time and all space. מהלּל <hi type="italic">laudatum</hi> (<hi type="italic">est</hi>), is equivalent to ἀινετόν, <hi type="italic">laudabile</hi> (lxx, Vulgate), and this does not differ greatly from <hi type="italic">laudetur</hi>. The predictive interpretation <hi type="italic">laudabitur</hi> is opposed to the context (cf. moreover Köhler on Mal 1:11).
entries.fb1d198900ae436f6a1931a9af6fd0785244f866: <reference osisRef="Ps.113.4-Ps.113.6">Psa 113:4-6</reference> <div eID="gen10087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10088" type="x-p"/> This praiseworthiness is now confirmed. The opening reminds one of Psa 99:2. <hi type="italic">Pasek</hi> stands between גוים and יהוה in order to keep them apart. The totality of the nations is great, but Jahve is raised above it; the heavens are glorious, but Jahve’s glory is exalted above them. It is not to be explained according to <reference osisRef="Ps.148.13">Psa 148:13</reference>; but according to <reference osisRef="Ps.57.6">Psa 57:6</reference>, 12, רם belongs to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.113.4">Psa 113:4</reference></hi> too as predicate. He is the incomparable One who has set up His throne in the height, but at the same time directs His gaze deep downwards (expression according to Ges. §142, rem. 1) in the heavens and upon earth, i.e., nothing in all the realm of the creatures that are beneath Him escapes His sight, and nothing is so low that it remains unnoticed by Him; on the contrary, it is just that which is lowly, as the following strophe presents to us in a series of portraits so to speak, that is the special object of His regard. The structure of <reference osisRef="Ps.113.5-Ps.113.6">Psa 113:5-6</reference> militates against the construction of “in the heavens and upon the earth” with the interrogatory “who is like unto Jahve our God?” after Deu 3:24.
entries.9ad9f7f3dd47b5c31d09efee190fd56b2ece5796: <reference osisRef="Ps.113.7-Ps.113.9">Psa 113:7-9</reference> <div eID="gen10088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10089" type="x-p"/> The thoughts of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.113.7">Psa 113:7</reference></hi> and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.113.8">Psa 113:8</reference></hi> are transplanted from the song of Hannah. עפר, according to 1Ki 16:2, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.14.7">Psa 14:7</reference>, is an emblem of lowly estate (Hitzig), and אשׁפּת (from שׁפת) an emblem of the deepest poverty and desertion; for in Syria and Palestine the man who is shut out from society lies upon the <hi type="italic">mezbele</hi> (the dunghill or heap of ashes), by day calling upon the passers-by for alms, and by night hiding himself in the ashes that have been warmed by the sun (<hi type="italic">Job</hi>, ii. 152). The movement of the thoughts in <reference osisRef="Ps.113.8">Psa 113:8</reference>, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.113.1">Psa 113:1</reference>, follows the model of the epizeuxis. Together with the song of Hannah the poet has before his eye Hannah’s exaltation out of sorrow and reproach. He does not, however, repeat the words of her song which have reference to this (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.5">1Sa 2:5</reference>), but clothes his generalization of her experience in his own language. If he intended that עקרת should be understood out of the genitival relation after the form עטרת, why did he not write מושׁיבי הבּית עקרה? הבּית would then be equivalent to בּיתה, Psa 68:7. עקרת הבּית is the expression for a woman who is a wife, and therefore housewife, הבּית (בּעלת) נות, but yet not a mother. Such an one has no settled position in the house of the husband, the firm bond is wanting in her relationship to her husband. If God gives her children, He thereby makes her then thoroughly at home and rooted-in in her position. In the predicate notion אם הבּנים שׂמחה the definiteness attaches to the second member of the string of words, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.48.19">Gen 48:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.30">2Sa 12:30</reference> (cf. the reverse instance in <reference osisRef="Jer.23.26">Jer 23:26</reference>, נבּאי השּׁקר, those prophesying that which is false), therefore: a mother of the children. The poet brings the matter so vividly before him, that he points as it were with his finger to the children with which God blesses her.  <chapter eID="Ps.113"/> <div eID="gen10089" type="x-p"/>

entries.71830d561e4ef817273a6705e42eae1675b48112:
PSALM 113
In this psalm the providence of God furnishes matter for praising him, because, though his excellency is far above the heavens, nevertheless, he deigns to cast his eyes upon the earth to take notice of mankind. And as not a few are disconcerted by the vicissitudes which they behold occurring in the world, the prophet takes occasion, from these sudden and unlooked for changes, to warn us to attend expressly to God’s providence, that we may entertain no doubt that all things are governed according to his will and pleasure.
This interesting little ode, which is alike elegant in its structure, and devotional in its sentiment, its theme being the celebration of Jehovah’s power, glory, and mercy, is thought by Bishop Patrick to be the commencement of what the Hebrews called the Great Hallel or Hymns, which they recited at their tables in the new moons and other feasts, especially in the paschal night, after they had eaten the lamb. He supposes that the Great Hallel included this and the five following psalms. See page 310. “It is very uncertain who was the author of this psalm; but as the 7th and 8th verses are manifestly taken from 1 Samuel 2:8, and the 9th probably alludes to the history of Hannah, it might be composed by Samuel or David, who were so nearly interested in the signal mercies vouchsafed to her.” — Dimock.
Psalm 113:1-4
1. Praise ye Jehovah. Praise, ye servants of Jehovah! praise the name of Jehovah. 2. Blessed be the name of Jehovah henceforth and for ever. 3. Jehovah’s name is to be praised, from the rising of the sun unto his going down. 4. Jehovah is high above all nations, his glory is above the heavens.
 
1 Praise, ye servants of Jehovah! This psalm contains abundant reasons for all men without exception to praise God. The faithful alone being endued with spiritual perception to recognize the hand of God, the prophet addresses them in particular. And if we consider how cold and callous men are in this religious exercise, we will not deem the repetition of the call to praise God superfluous. We all acknowledge that we are created to praise God’s name, while, at the same time, his glory is disregarded by us. Such criminal apathy is justly condemned by the prophet, with the view of stirring us up to unwearied zeal in praising God. The repetition, then, of the exhortation to praise him, ought to be considered as referring both to perseverance and ardor in this service. If, by the servants of God, some would rather understand the Levites, to whom the charge of celebrating his praises under the Law was committed, I am not much opposed to it, provided they do not exclude the rest of the faithful, over whom formerly God appointed the Levites as leaders and chief musicians, that he might be praised by all his people without exception. When the Holy Spirit addresses the Levites expressly in relation to the subject of God’s praises, it is designedly that, by their example, they may show the way to others, and that the whole Church may respond in one holy chorus. Now that we are all “a royal priesthood,” (1 Peter 2:9) and as Zechariah testifies, (Zechariah 14:21) that under the reign of Christ, the meanest of the people shall be Levites, there is no question that, excepting unbelievers who are mute, the prophet invites us all in common to render this service unto God.
